summary.text: A vector space is a set whose elements, called vectors, can be added together and scaled by numbers called scalars, following rules known as the vector axioms.
Vector spaces generalize Euclidean vectors, which model physical quantities such as forces and velocity that have both a magnitude and a direction.
Every vector space has a dimension, roughly the number of independent directions, and all bases of the space have that same size.

paragraphs.heading: Things you can add and scale
paragraphs.text: In mathematics, a vector is a member of a vector space, also called a linear space. A vector space is a set whose members can be added to each other and multiplied, or scaled, by numbers. Those numbers are called scalars. The two operations have to obey a list of rules known as the vector axioms.

paragraphs.heading: From arrows to abstraction
paragraphs.text: Vector spaces are a generalization of Euclidean vectors. Those are used to model physical quantities like force and velocity, which have a size as well as a direction. When the scalars are real numbers you get a real vector space, and when they are complex numbers you get a complex vector space. These two are the most common, but the scalars can come from any field.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Vector spaces sit at the heart of linear algebra. Together with matrices, which let you compute inside a vector space, they give a compact way to handle and study systems of linear equations. Vector spaces also turn up across mathematics, often with extra structure added on top, as in Hilbert spaces and Banach spaces.

paragraphs.heading: Building with combinations
paragraphs.text: Take some vectors, scale each by a number, and add the results: that is a linear combination, and the numbers are its coefficients. A set of vectors is linearly independent when none of them can be built as a linear combination of the others. The span of a set is everything you can build from it with linear combinations. A linear subspace is a part of the space that stays closed: adding two of its members, or scaling one, never takes you outside it.

paragraphs.heading: Basis and dimension
paragraphs.text: A basis is a set of vectors that is linearly independent and also spans the whole space. Every vector space has at least one basis, and usually many. All of them have the same size, and that size is the dimension of the space. Roughly, the dimension counts how many independent directions the space has.

paragraphs.heading: When dimension is infinite
paragraphs.text: If the dimension is a natural number, the space is finite-dimensional; these show up naturally in geometry. If not, the space is infinite-dimensional. Polynomials give an example: the polynomial rings form vector spaces with countably infinite dimension. A striking consequence of dimension is that two vector spaces over the same field with the same dimension behave exactly alike as vector spaces, which mathematicians say by calling them isomorphic.
